content: The combination of the simps attribute and the dsimp tactic seems to be currently broken. In the following example, simps seems to fail to register rfl-lemmas as defeq.

module

public import Mathlib.CategoryTheory.Adjunction.Basic

@[expose] public section

namespace CategoryTheory.Adjunction

variable (C : Type*) [Category* C]

@[simps]
def id' : 𝟭 C ⊣ 𝟭 C where
  unit := (Functor.rightUnitor (𝟭 C)).inv
  counit := (Functor.rightUnitor (𝟭 C)).hom

lemma test : (Adjunction.id' C).unit = (Functor.rightUnitor (𝟭 C)).inv := by
  simp only [id'_unit]

lemma test2 : (Adjunction.id' C).unit = (Functor.rightUnitor (𝟭 C)).inv := by
  dsimp only [id'_unit] -- fails
  -- but would succeed if we explicitly do `attribute [defeq] id'_unit`

set_option backward.defeqAttrib.useBackward true in
lemma test2' : (Adjunction.id' C).unit = (Functor.rightUnitor (𝟭 C)).inv := by
  dsimp only [id'_unit] -- succeeds

@[simp]
lemma id'_unit' : (id' C).unit = (Functor.rightUnitor (𝟭 C)).inv := rfl

lemma test3 : (Adjunction.id' C).unit = (Functor.rightUnitor (𝟭 C)).inv := by
  dsimp only [id'_unit'] -- succeeds

end CategoryTheory.Adjunction

I found this while investigating the change https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blame/5027efbcc182a92a717b256053b9b0319ca6aada/Mathlib/Topology/Convenient/Category.lean#L206 in #39980 where a very reasonable proof by dsimp; infer_instance was replaced by inferInstanceAs ....
See also #37528.
How is this relevant? Could you explain where there is a defeq abuse in the code above???

Even with the code in #37258, no warning is generated on that @[simps], and I also fail to see where there is any form of abuse here (especially since @[defeq] is correctly added on the second lemma id_unit'! edit: set_option simp.rfl.checkTransparency true emits a warning about it: it might just be that id' is a def) , but setting Adjunction.id' with implicit_reducible here lets the lemma be @[defeq] as expected so it has to do with transparency.

Joël Riou said:

How is this relevant? Could you explain where there is a defeq abuse in the code above???

Your definition is semireducible, therefore its projections are only semireducibly defeq to their values. Yes, this impacts basically all projections ever. Expect dsimp's use case to shift a lot.
My conclusion is that dsimp is completely broken. What is the point of a tactic that can only substitute a = a, i.e. do nothing?

module

public import Mathlib.Data.Nat.Notation
public import Mathlib.Tactic.Simps.Basic

@[expose] public section

structure Foo where
  l : ℕ

@[simps]
def foo : Foo where
  l := 42

example : foo.l = 42 := by simp

example : foo.l = 42 := by dsimp -- fails
Ooof, @Kim Morrison is this intended/expected?
I think this is by design... Unfortunately, Joachim is away in Canada on a long vacation now, and we really need to hear from him, I think.

I would understand that dsimp would be reluctant to replace an equality rfl : x = y when x : A and y : B and A and B do not perfectly match at a certain transparency level, but in the examples above A and B are just the same.
If this is the intended behaviour, could someone implement a edsimp tactic which would be simp only [all rfl lemmas]?

The problem is that simp only [all rfl lemmas] has very different behaviour, because it needs congruence lemmas to rewrite in dependent positions, whereas a dsimp can just do the replacement without a proof.

Sorry, that's not quite right: of course simp switches to dsimp mode automatically, but ... I think this means you still run into the same problem.

Joël Riou said:

I would understand that dsimp would be reluctant to replace an equality rfl : x = y when x : A and y : B and A and B do not perfectly match at a certain transparency level, but in the examples above A and B are just the same.

It's not really about the types here. If we have any dependent arguments, dsimping by foo.l = 42 will create something that doesn't typecheck except at default transparency.

(Caveats here, I'm not on top of these dsimp changes myself, so please expect mistakes about either implementation details or motivations in what I say!)
This seems expected to me. Eg you don't want dsimp to turn Fin foo.l into Fin 42. That would be defeq abuse.

What I am asking is a tactic that does what the previous dsimp was doing. It could be the current dsimp with a suitable set_option or, as it was discussed somewhere else, it may be implemented using simp.

Johan Commelin said:

Ooof, Kim Morrison is this intended/expected?

I am pretty sure that this is intended. @Eric Wieser posted an isomorphic MWE in the nightly testing stream (#nightly-testing > lean#13492, stricter @[defeq] inference @ 💬 ) for this change and Joachim confirmed that.
I guess dsimp could have different behavior depending on whether it's rewriting inside a type or not, but this looks complicated

I think the unfolding strategy that @Mario Carneiro mentioned during the retreat is worth considering further. Even if it isn't part of the defeq-check in the kernel, it seems like a tactic that could profitably live in user space?

Concerning Joël's original example, I am still confused though why the behaviour of @[simps] and plain @[simp] differs. In other words, why does the following work?

structure Foo where
  l : Nat

def foo : Foo where
  l := 42

@[simp]
theorem foo_l : foo.l = 42 := rfl

example : foo.l = 42 := by dsimp

Yes, that certainly looks like @[simps] needs updating --- I really thought we had already done this. I have two PRs on simps open that got lost in the shuffle, but neither seem to address this issue.
(Running out of time now, but it looks fixable, I'll try to get this done later tonight.)

I think it is just that in simps we should be calling markDefEq, instead of inferDefEqAttr... This would at least fix some symptoms, but I fear still goes against the intended design Joachim is aiming for!
So to make sure I understand correctly: @[simp] is calling markDefEq if the proof is := rfl and not inferDefEqAttr? So then, when is inferDefEqAttr ever used?

Sorry, I think I was confused above.

For user written lemmas, that have body syntactically := rfl, we use markDefEq:

  • apply @[defeq] if the lemma works at default transparency
  • fails with an error otherwise (shouldn't ever happen, because by this time the rfl proof has been accepted)

For generated declarations, we use inferDefEqAttr, which looks at the proof term to decide if it is a rfl lemma, and then

  • applies @[defeq] if the lemma works at instance transparency
  • otherwise applies @[backward_defeq]

Currently, @[simps] uses inferDefEqAttr, although in #40112 you can see a PR that tries switching it to using the markDefEq mechanism (although can't actually call markDefEq itself) (entirely untested as yet).

I think that, according to Joachim's intention, the current behaviour of simps is correct, and #40112 is bad, and the set_option, or a different tactic, is appropriate if you want to dsimp by simps lemmas.

So then, if I understand Joachim's vision correctly, in the long term @[simp] should also use inferDefEqAttr instead of markDefEq? That would make the behaviour consistent (and dsimp even less useful in practice).

I think Joël Riou is right, that we need a tactic that calls simp only with all @[backward_defeq] lemmas (which would be mostly equivalent to the old dsimp behaviour). It might be called edsimp, or something else (edsimp reminds of the evil erw, which would be a wrong connotation, since this edsimp would not be evil). And maybe in the future when @[backward_defeq] gets deprecated, this should become a separate simp set that you would explicitly have to opt into (and we would make @[simps] lemmas opt in to this by default). And the idea of this simp set is to be a more reliable/robust subset of the standard simp set, so that it can be used in non-terminal positions (just like we allow with dsimp now).
rflsimp?

Johan Commelin said:

I think the unfolding strategy that Mario Carneiro mentioned during the retreat is worth considering further. Even if it isn't part of the defeq-check in the kernel, it seems like a tactic that could profitably live in user space?

I would be keen to hear more about this.

The only thing that I don't like about the edsimp proposal is that it adds yet another tactic beginners need to learn about. What is the future use case of dsimp in its current (i.e. without the magic option) form in mathlib? Can edsimp just be the default behaviour in mathlib?

Kim Morrison said:

I think that, according to Joachim's intention, the current behaviour of simps is correct, and #40112 is bad, and the set_option, or a different tactic, is appropriate if you want to dsimp by simps lemmas.

Are there plans to make the following example (also posted by Christian Merten above) fail?

structure Foo where
  l : Nat

def foo : Foo where
  l := 42

@[simp] theorem foo_def : foo.l = 42 := rfl

example : foo.l = 42 := by dsimp -- succeeds

@[simps] was intended to automatically generate these simple (mostly)-rfl lemmas for structure projections. If the example above is intended to succeed, I don't see why tagging foo with @[simps] should behave any differently.
My understanding is that it should fail in the future, because dsimp is only supposed to apply lemmas that hold at reducible transparency, which this lemma does not.

To quote Joachim again:
Joachim Breitner said in #nightly-testing > lean#13492, stricter @[defeq] inference:

This PR does not do that yet, but in a follow up we plan to apply the same discipline to := rfl lemmas and theorems explicitly marked as @[defeq].

My understanding of dsimp is that it could be used for either "trivial rewrites" like x ∈ {y | p y} to p x, or for type rewrites. Presumably the latter is now off the table now that we're being stricter about def-eqs. Would it be sound to keep the former functionality? i.e. keeping dsimp as a weaker simp that we're fine with not being terminal.

Yes exactly. The situation is awkward because dsimp can mean different things:

  1. Unlike simp, simplify in arbitrary places in the given expression. To ensure the result is still sensible, we can only do rewrites that hold definitionally in with_reducible_and_instances. This is dsimp
  2. Run simp only with the set of lemmas that just so happen to hold definitionally (but don't rewrite in dependent positions). This is the hypothetical new rflsimp/edsimp
(deleted)
If I read lean4#13492 right, we already have set_option backward.defeqAttrib.useBackward true in dsimp as an edsimp workaround, right?
Oh, but then we'd be back at rewriting in dependent positions. So we'd need to maintain a separate simp set somehow. I see now why this is hard!
So there's no easy way to create a tactic that does what dsimp used to do 2 months ago?

What it used to do 2 months ago, we get with the useBackward. But this is not what we really want: we want to use the .instances-level defeq lemmas in dependent positions and .default-level defeq lemmas in non-dependent positions.

It would be relatively easy to get something that does that, I think. You'd take the docs#SimpTheoremArray passed to edsimp, create a new one by filtering for those that have docs#Lean.Meta.SimpTheorem.rfl or docs#Lean.Meta.SimpTheorem.backwardRfl, and pass that set into simp (or maybe simp -dsimp?). Drawback is this gives a huge upfront cost (namely, O(N log N) or so where N is number of all @[simp] lemmas) to all edsimp calls.

Making a performant version would be a lot of hassle: the right point to do this filtering is in the middle of the simp algorithm when we have collected all lemmas matching the discrimination tree key, and deciding whether we want to apply them. In other words the check right here should distinguish between dsimp mode, edsimp mode and simp mode.

Anne Baanen said:

What it used to do 2 months ago, we get with the useBackward. But this is not what we really want: [...]

My impression from @Joël Riou is that already the twoMonthsAgo_dsimp tactic would be useful to have as part of the toolkit. At least as a stopgap, until better and more subtle scalpels become available.

If I understand @Kim Morrison correctly, for any further changes in core on this we need to wait for Joachim to return from his (long?) vacation.
How about setting set_option backward.defeqAttrib.useBackward true globally in mathlibs lakefile in the meantime and come back to this discussion when Joachim is back?

Should we just create a new simp set for this rflsimp tactic now and start tagging things (in particular, start with auto-tagging all simps lemmas)? This way, we can get started with removing these backward.defeqAttrib.useBackward options that have just landed in mathlib.
And this would include writing a rflsimp% elaborator that takes the role of the previous dsimp% elaborator.
Is it possible to hook into the elaboration of @[simp] to also add to the rflsimp simp set if the proof is rfl?

Christian Merten said:

if the proof is rfl

Would this be based on the syntax of the proof, or the value of the proof? I.e. does a proof := (rfl) count?

Jovan Gerbscheid said:

Christian Merten said:

if the proof is rfl

Would this be based on the syntax of the proof, or the value of the proof? I.e. does a proof := (rfl) count?

Currently, these is a difference between := rfl and := by rfl.

Actually, now that I think of it, we don't need to re-do the check. We can add a hook to the @[simp] tag so that after applying the tag, we check whether the lemma got the backward_defeq attribute, and if so, then we add the lemma to the rflsimp simpset.
